value: Matthew was buried in the Avonlea graveyard
unit: Matthew Cuthbert lived at Green Gables with his unmarried sister, Marilla. Intending to adopt an orphan boy to assist with farmwork, Matthew drove to Bright River station only to find eleven-year-old Anne Shirley waiting instead. Touched by her chatter and imaginative spirit during the drive home, Matthew quietly insisted to Marilla that they keep her. Over the following years, he became Anne's steadfast supporter, giving her a gift of a fashionable dress with puffed sleeves for Christmas and encouraging her academic pursuits. As he aged, he suffered from severe heart trouble and worked beyond his physical capacity. After learning of the sudden failure of the Abbey Bank where all his savings were deposited, Matthew collapsed and died instantly of the shock. He was buried in the Avonlea graveyard, where Anne continued to visit his grave long after his passing.

label: History
value: Rachel did not move out West with her children
unit: Mrs. Rachel Lynde lived in Lynde's Hollow on the Avonlea main road, where she kept close watch over everything passing by while running local church societies and knitting quilts. When Matthew Cuthbert brought orphan Anne Shirley to Green Gables, Rachel was astonished and visited to inspect her; her blunt criticism of Anne's freckles and red hair sparked a fiery temper outburst from the girl. After Anne delivered a dramatic apology, Rachel forgave her, allowed her to pick lilies in her garden, and gradually grew to admire her progress and beauty over the years. Following a severe illness with the grippe, Rachel continued her energetic community work, including heading church bazaars, political rallies, and advising Marilla Cuthbert on raising children. When her meek husband Thomas fell ill and passed away, Rachel was forced to sell their mortgaged farm. Rather than move out West with her children or live with her daughter Eliza, she accepted Marilla's invitation to move into Green Gables to live together. She continued supervising household life at Green Gables, helping care for the adopted twins Davy and Dora Keith, and attending church events despite occasional accidents like twisting her ankle or falling down cellar stairs. Years later, she happily helped prepare for Anne's wedding to Gilbert Blythe at Green Gables, bringing homemade gifts and plum pudding to visit Anne and Gilbert in Four Winds for Christmas.

I was vain and coquettish and liked to tease him a little. He was a very high-strung, sensitive fellow. Well, we parted in a temper on both sides. But I thought it would all come right; and it would have if Stephen hadn’t come back too soon. Anne, my dear, I’m sorry to say” . . . Miss Lavendar dropped her voice as if she were about to confess a predilection for murdering people, “that I am a dreadfully sulky person. Oh, you needn’t smile, . . . it’s only too true. I do sulk; and Stephen came back before I had finished sulking. I wouldn’t listen to him and I wouldn’t forgive him; and so he went away for good. He was too proud to come again. And then I sulked because he didn’t come. I might have sent for him perhaps, but I couldn’t humble myself to do that. I was just as proud as he was . . . pride and sulkiness make a very bad combination, Anne. But I could never care for anybody else and I didn’t want to. I knew I would rather be an old maid for a thousand years than marry anybody who wasn’t Stephen Irving. Well, it all seems like a dream now, of course. How sympathetic you look, Anne . . . as sympathetic as only seventeen can look. But don’t overdo it. I’m really a very happy, contented little person in spite of my broken heart. My heart did break, if ever a heart did, when I realized that Stephen Irving was not coming back. But, Anne, a broken heart in real life isn’t half as dreadful as it is in books. It’s a good deal like a bad tooth . . . though you won’t think that a very romantic simile. It takes spells of aching and gives you a sleepless night now and then, but between times it lets you enjoy life and dreams and echoes and peanut candy as if there were nothing the matter with it. And now you’re looking disappointed. You don’t think I’m half as interesting a person as you did five minutes ago when you believed I was always the prey of a tragic memory bravely hidden beneath external smiles. That’s the worst . . . or the best . . . of real life, Anne. It won’t let you be miserable. It keeps on trying to make you comfortable . . . and succeeding...even when you’re determined to be unhappy and romantic. Isn’t this candy scrumptious? I’ve eaten far more than is good for me already but I’m going to keep recklessly on.”
